title: Never break faith
hookLine: value nothing that makes you break your word or lose self-respect (Meditations 3.7)

cards: Curtains can tell you something about a house. Some hang there for warmth, or for sleep.
And sometimes a curtain is there for another reason: the purchase nobody mentioned, the deleted message, the plan someone would rather nobody saw. Marcus Aurelius used curtains as a test.
In the seventh entry of his third book he lists what a person should never count as worth having, and he ends the list with walls and curtains. Today: never break faith.

teach.h: NEVER COUNT IT A GAIN IF IT COSTS YOUR WORD.
teach.b: Never value anything as good for you, Marcus writes, if it will one day force you to break your word or lose your self-respect. Notice the order. He doesn't start with what's forbidden; he starts with what we value.
If a thing would cost you your word, it was never really a gain.
The list goes on: nothing that makes you hate anyone, suspect anyone, curse anyone, play the hypocrite. Each is a small way of breaking faith, with another person or with yourself.

teach.h: NOTHING THAT NEEDS WALLS AND CURTAINS.
teach.b: It ends with anything you'd want that needs walls and curtains around it. A plain household test: if a desire only works in hiding, Marcus counts it a loss, however good it looks.
It echoes the test from two days ago: think only what you could say out loud.
Then he sketches the person who keeps faith. They put their own mind and its goodness first. They don't make a tragedy of things, don't groan, and need neither solitude nor a crowd.
They neither chase life nor run from it.
Breaking faith is rarely one big betrayal. It's usually small: the call you said you'd make, the favor you said you'd do, the time you said you'd be there.
A word that holds in small things is easier to trust in large ones. That's what Marcus is protecting: not a reputation, but a self you can respect.

how: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius treat Meditations 3.7 as a household test: if a desire only works in hiding, behind walls and curtains, they count it as a loss.

o: the emperor who said never value what costs you your word
a Greek teacher who said oaths bind only the gods
a Roman general who wrote the laws on broken contracts

p: neither chases life nor runs from it
usually small, not one big betrayal

s: Marcus starts with a list of forbidden acts
he starts with what we value: never count as a gain what costs your word.
Marcus counts hating and suspecting as ways to break faith
they're on his list beside cursing and playing the hypocrite.
Marcus says the faithful person needs solitude
he says they need neither solitude nor a crowd.

games.q: a coworker offers to cover for you if you skip the meeting you promised to lead. nobody would know. what fits 3.7?
o: keep the promise and lead the meeting.
skip it, but tell yourself it's fine.
games.why: Marcus counts nothing a gain that costs your word, and a plan that needs hiding fails his walls-and-curtains test.

practice: Think of one promise that's still open, even a tiny one, like I'll call you back or I'll be there at six, and picture the person who heard you say it.
Picture keeping it plainly, without fuss, and rest a moment in what it's like to be someone whose word holds.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, whose rule was to value nothing that would cost your word, your self-respect, or something that needs walls and curtains. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'faith, trust, a pledge': the word for the faith Marcus says never to break.

carryVoice: Your line: keep faith. Nothing worth having needs walls and curtains around it. Until tomorrow.
